**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 2:**

﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

This is an *isti'naf ibtida'i* (a fresh, independent resumptive sentence) and it is a nominal clause made up of a *mubtada'* (subject) and a *khabar* (predicate).

"The Book" (al-Kitab) refers to the known one, namely what had been revealed of the Qur'an up to that moment.

The purpose is to establish that the Qur'an is revealed by Allah to His Messenger ﷺ. Strictly speaking, the apparent requirement was that the Qur'an be made the subject and be described, so that it would be said: "The Qur'an is revealed from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." This is because its being revealed from Allah is the point of dispute, so it should be the predicate. Had they accepted that it is a revelation, there would be no disagreement among them that its revelation is from Allah. But the apparent order was departed from for two purposes:

The first: to create eagerness to receive the predicate. When they heard the opening with "the revelation of the Book," they would look forward to what would be said about it. As for the disbelievers, they would anticipate that some new description of the circumstances of the revelation of the Book would be conveyed to them, so they would prepare for a fresh round of their disputing and obstinacy. The believers would be waiting for what would increase their certainty regarding this revelation.

The second purpose: to assert that the Qur'an's being a revelation is a matter on which there is no disagreement. Those who opposed it are as though they opposed its being sent down from Allah, and surely revelation is only from Allah. Thus it returns to emphasizing the report that it is revealed from Allah, since there is no difference between the meaning of "being a revelation" and "being from Allah," except in the difference of the concepts of the two meanings, not in their referent. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 26].

The choice of mentioning the two attributes "the Mighty, the Wise" rather than other of the Beautiful Names is to indicate, through the attribute of "the Mighty," that what was revealed from Him is fitting to His might; so it is a "mighty Book," as He described it: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾ [Fussilat: 41], meaning that it prevails over its opponents, because it has rendered them unable to produce its like. And through the attribute of "the Wise," it indicates that what was revealed from Him is fitting to His wisdom; so it comprises proofs of certainty and truth. In this there is an allusion that its inimitability is from two aspects: from the aspect of its eloquence, since the eloquence of its eloquent people was overcome by it; and from the aspect of its meanings, since its wisdom rendered the wisdom of the wise incapable of matching it.

This is because the signs in the heavens and the earth, and what is joined to them, are signs only for the believers who are certain, and for those who have gained knowledge through what the Qur'an reminded them of. Supporting this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿These are the signs of Allah which We recite to you﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 6].

It is emphasized with *inna* (indeed), although the addressees were not deniers of it. Their situation was treated as that of deniers, because of their failure to benefit from the evidence in these created beings for the oneness of Allah, exalted is He. Otherwise Allah, exalted is He, has said, ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9] in Surat al-Zukhruf.

The address is directed to the polytheists, and therefore He said ﴿Indeed, there are signs for the believers﴾ and said ﴿signs for a people who are certain﴾, rather than saying "indeed there are signs for you" or "signs for you". That is, these are signs for those among the believers who know their indication. The phrase "among those who are certain" points to the fact that those signs have no effect on the souls of those who are otherwise.

The meaning of the signs being "in the heavens and the earth" is that the very substance of the heavens and the earth, and the enumeration of their attributes, are indications of the oneness (*wahdaniyya*) of Allah. Thus the heavens and the earth are placed as a container (*zarf*) for what has been deposited in them of signs, because these are inseparable from them to anyone who looks even briefly. The signs were attributed to "the believers" because they are the ones who benefited from their indication and learned from them that their Originator and the Ordainer of their order is one, with no partner.

The conjunction of the sentence ﴿And in your creation﴾ etc. to the sentence ﴿Indeed, in the heavens and the earth there are signs for the believers﴾ is a conjunction of the particular to the general (*'atf khass 'ala 'amm*), because this particular contains a reminder of the blessing of the creation of the species, calling for gratitude for it.

*Al-batth* means dispersal and multiplication, and it implies creation and origination. It is as if it were said: "And in the creation of Allah is what disperses of every creature." *Al-batth* was mentioned in His saying, ﴿and He dispersed in them every kind of creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah.

He expressed with the present tense in *yabuthu* (disperses) to indicate the continual renewal and recurrence of the dispersal, in terms of the variety of kinds, species, and types of creatures.

*Al-dabba* (creature) is applied to everything that crawls upon the earth other than humans; this is its original usage. It is also applied to what walks on feet, excluding birds, as in His saying, ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

*Al-rizq* (provision) is applied here to rain, by way of metonymy (*al-majaz al-mursal*, a figurative usage based on a related cause), because rain is the cause of the existence of sustenance. *Al-rizq* means nourishment. It was mentioned in the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, ﴿and what Allah sent down from the sky of water﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

Parallels to this verse have preceded in the middle of Surat al-Baqarah and in several other places.

What is meant by "the believers," "a people who are certain," and "a people who reason" is one and the same: they are the believers in the oneness of Allah. Certainty (*yaqin*) was attained by them, and they were people of reason, that is, they knew the indication of the signs.

The meaning is: the believers, and those who are certain, that is, who know and do not obstinately deny, and those who reason, that is, who understand the indication of effects upon their cause, and who looked with correct reflection at the evidences in the heavens and the earth, and so knew that they must have a maker and that He is one. Thus the rational person among them who was hesitant became certain of this, and the one who was already a believer increased in faith and became certain. So the meaning is that those who benefited from the signs are the believing and rational people. These attributes were distributed among the endings of these verses, because that is more striking to the listener's soul than repeating one of them in place of another.

The attribute of believing was placed first because of its nobility. The creation of humans and creatures was made a sign for those characterized by certainty, because the indication of creation lies within the human being himself and in the creatures surrounding him. The alternation of night and day, and the variation of atmospheric events, were made a sign for those characterized by reason, because their indication of oneness is through necessary consequences that are established by the perception of reason.

The mention of these attributes implies that those who were not guided by these signs are not among the possessors of these attributes. For this reason He followed it with His saying, ﴿Then in what discourse after Allah and His signs will they believe?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 6], as a rhetorical question of denial, meaning negation.

Know that although this statement is addressed to a people who do not deny the existence of God but ascribe partners to Him, and although its primary purpose was to establish the oneness at the outset, it is also suitable for establishing proof against the *mu'attilun* (deniers of divine attributes or of the Creator) who deny the existence of the Creator who chooses (*al-Sani' al-Mukhtar*). For all the states of the heavens are changing, indicating the change of what they are characterized by, and change is a proof of having come into being (*huduth*), which means the need for an agent who chooses, who brings them into existence after non-existence and then annihilates them.

The majority of readers recited His saying ﴿Indeed there are signs for a people who are certain﴾ and His saying ﴿signs for a people who reason﴾ with *ayat* in the nominative (*raf'*) in both places, taking them as subjects (*mubtada'*), with the prepositional phrases as their predicates (*khabar*). The preposition *fi* (in) is considered elided in His saying ﴿and in the alternation of night and day﴾, because its sister preposition in His saying ﴿and in your creation﴾ indicates it.

The conjunction in both sentences is a conjunction of whole sentences, not a conjunction of single words.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read *ayat* in both places with a kasra in place of the fatha. Thus the first *ayat* is conjoined to the subject of *inna*, and "in your creation" is conjoined to the predicate of *inna*. The correct view is that of the majority of the Kufans, and it is so common that it rejects interpretation. Ibn al-Hajib, in his *Amali*, considered the majority reading with *raf'* of *ayat* in both places also to be a conjunction to two complements of two governing words, because the nominative needs a governing word just as the accusative needs one. He said: "Most people raise the difficulty in the reading of the accusative because its governing word is verbal, though the two are equal." Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 6:

﴿These are the signs of Allah, which We recite to you in truth. Then in what discourse after Allah and His signs will they believe?﴾

It is permissible that the demonstrative reference ("these") and its explanation by "the signs of Allah" refer to the signs mentioned in His saying ﴿Surely there are signs for the believers﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 3], and His saying ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who believe﴾ [al-An'am: 99], and His saying ﴿signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 5].

Its attribution to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is because its Creator is upon those attributes which made them signs for those who seek guidance.

The clause ﴿which We recite to you in truth﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the signs of Allah." The governing element in the demonstrative is the meaning of a verb, in the manner of His saying Exalted is He ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72].

Al-tilawah means recitation (al-qira'ah). The meaning of the signs being "recited" is that in the recited words of the Qur'an there is an indication of them; so the use of the verb "natlu" (We recite) is a metaphor of the rational kind (majaz 'aqli), since what is recited is that which indicates them.

It is also permissible that the demonstrative refers to something present in the mind but not mentioned, indicated by His saying "the Book," meaning: these are the signs of Allah sent down in the Qur'an. In that case the use of the verb "natluha" is in its literal sense.

Attributing the recitation to Allah is also a metaphor of the rational kind, since Allah is the originator of the recited Qur'an which points to those signs.

His saying ﴿Then in what discourse after Allah and His signs will they believe?﴾: here "ba'da" (after) is in the sense of "dūna" (apart from). The meaning is: "Then in what discourse apart from Allah and His signs?" His saying Exalted is He ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾ [al-Shura: 44] has preceded in Surat al-Shura, and in al-A'raf: ﴿Then in what discourse after it will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185]. **Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 11:**

﴿This is guidance. And those who disbelieve in the signs of their Lord — for them is a punishment of a painful, wretched affliction.﴾

The clause "This is guidance" is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which the discourse shifts from describing the Qur'an in itself — that it is sent down from Allah and that it is among the signs of Allah — to describing it by its most excellent attribute, that it is guidance. The demonstrative "This" (hadha) refers to the Qur'an as it is at the time of its revelation and recitation, so it is like something present before the eye. Moreover, its attributes have already preceded, such as His saying ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 2] and His saying ﴿These are the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 6] and so on to the end, which made it distinct and individual, so that the demonstrative reference to it is well-suited.

Describing the Qur'an as "guidance" is an attribution by way of the verbal noun (wasf bi-l-masdar) for emphasis (mubalaghah), meaning: a guide for people. Whoever believes in it has been guided, and whoever disbelieves in it, for him is a punishment, because he has deprived himself of guidance, so he remains in error and is immersed in corruption and sins.

The clause "And those who disbelieve" is coordinated (atf) upon the clause "This is guidance." The connection is that the Qur'an is among the signs of Allah and is a reminder of them, so those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah have disbelieved in the Qur'an as one of the general signs. This stands in the position of a conclusion (tadhyil) to what precedes it from His saying ﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 7].

The relative pronoun with its relative clause (al-mawsul wa silatuhu) is used because of what the relative clause indicates: that they are deserving of punishment.

In this context they are referred to by the title of disbelief (al-kufr), rather than the two titles of persistence and arrogance by which they were referred to in His saying ﴿Then he persists, arrogant﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 8]. This is because the purpose here is to censure them for neglecting to benefit from the Qur'an, which is the greatest blessing that came to them from Allah, and they responded to it with disbelief in place of gratitude, as He, exalted, says ﴿And you make your provision [to be] that you deny﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82].

"Al-rijz" means the most severe punishment. The Exalted said ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the sky because they were defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59].

The particle "min" (in min rijzin) may be explanatory (li-l-bayan), so that the punishment is the rijz; or it may be partitive (li-l-tab'id), meaning a punishment of the kind called rijz, namely its most severe form.

"Alim" (painful) may be an adjective of "'adhab" (punishment), in which case it is in the nominative, and this is how the majority (al-Jumhur) read it. It may also be an adjective of "rijz," in which case it is in the genitive, as Ibn Kathir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 12:

﴿It is Allah who subjected the sea to you, that the ships may sail upon it by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may give thanks.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) marking a transition from the reminder of the creatures Allah created and the varying states of those creatures, insofar as they are indications of God's oneness, to the reminder of the creatures and their varying states that Allah subjected for the people, insofar as the benefits of the people require that they give thanks to the One who determined them.

Yet they denied these [benefits] when they directed worship to other than the One who bestowed them upon them. For this reason, the verb "sakhkhara" (subjected) in both places is linked, through the preposition of purpose (lam al-'illa) in the word "lakum" (for you). Moreover, these varying states are also signs, like the alternation of night and day, the water Allah sends down from the sky, and the turning of the winds. But here what is considered is the blessings they contain, just as there what was considered was the indication they contain. The discerning person draws both matters from both contexts, in a manner resembling ihtibak (complementary omission). The connection of this transition is clear.

The name of Allah (ism al-jalala) is the subject (musnad ilayhi), and the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the predicate (musnad). The definiteness of both parts conveys restriction (hasr), and it is a qasr qalb (restriction by reversal), by treating the polytheists as those who think that the subjecting of the sea and the subjecting of what is in the heavens and the earth is a favor from their partners, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ [al-Rum: 40]. So this restriction was a refutation of this claim which this structure implied.

His saying ﴿that the ships may sail upon it﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "lakum" (for you), because in His saying "lakum" there is a general statement whose detail is intended.

The definite article in "al-fulk" (the ships) is the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). The sailing of ships upon the sea is not a blessing upon people except in terms of their carrying the ships for travel on the sea. So there is no need to make the alif and lam a substitute for the omitted genitive (iwad 'an al-mudaf ilayhi), in the manner of ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41].

His saying ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is coordinated with it on the basis of the general inclusiveness it contains. From the totality of this it results that the subjecting of the sea for the sailing of ships upon it is for travel to fulfill various needs, even recreation and visiting family.

His saying ﴿and that you may give thanks﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿that the ships may sail upon it﴾, not on the basis of what it includes in general, but on the basis of its wording in its dependence on its verb. This is the purpose of the context of this speech, meaning: "that you may give thanks," but you denied. ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him.﴾ This is a generalization following a restriction, which was required first by the emphasis (al-ihtimam) and then by the generalization that follows. "Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" is a general term restricted to those things from whose existence people derive benefit, such as the sun for light and rain for drink, or from some of their conditions, such as the stars for guidance by them in the darknesses of land and sea, trees for shade, and livestock for riding, ploughing, and the like. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾

That is, in what has been mentioned, namely the subjection of the sea and the subjection of whatever is in the heavens and the earth, there are proofs of Allah's singularity in divinity. Although these are favours that people should rightly thank Him for, they are also proofs, by which those who are favoured are guided when they reflect upon them. Thus they gain from them both bodily benefits and intellectual knowledge. In this sense they are counted among the signs mentioned before it in His words ﴿Indeed, in the heavens and the earth are signs for the believers﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 3]. They were placed after those signs because they were mentioned in the context of granting favour, that they are blessings, and then they were followed by an admonition that they are also proofs of Allah's singularity in creation.

"Reflection" (tafakkur) was chosen to be mentioned last among the attributes of those who derive proof from the signs, because reflection is the source of faith, certainty, and knowledge, which were mentioned earlier in His words ﴿signs for the believers﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 3], ﴿signs for a people who believe﴾ [Al-An'am: 99], and ﴿signs for a people who understand﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 14–15 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the Days of Allah, so that He may recompense a people for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self; and whoever does evil, it is against it. Then to your Lord you will be returned.﴾

If this (verse) is connected in revelation to the verses before it, and what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning its occasion of revelation is not authentic, then the reason for its placement here is that His saying ﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 7] up to His saying ﴿For them is a painful punishment of wretchedness﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 11] stirs the anger of the Muslims against those who mock the Qur'an.

The Muslims had begun to take pride in their numbers, and so the mention of the polytheists' mockery of the Qur'an and their arrogance in refusing to hear it was likely to lead some Muslims to strike out at some polytheists. It is also possible that some Muslims had shown anger or a threat, and that Allah knew this from some of them.

Al-Qurtubi and al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the people of Makkah, who suffered severe harm from the polytheists, so they complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ. Allah then commanded them to overlook that, for the benefit of preserving calm in Makkah and of mutual disengagement between the Muslims and the polytheists. In this there are many benefits, among them the spread of the Qur'an among the people of Makkah and among the tribes living around it; for its spread cannot avoid seizing their hearts, despite their outward aversion, arrogance and mockery. Thus their souls would be prepared to enter the religion once the obstruction of their chiefs was removed, after the Hijrah of the Prophet ﷺ to Madinah and after the destruction of the leaders of Quraysh at the Battle of Badr.

Similar commands to pardon and forgive the polytheists and to turn away from their harm are repeated in the Qur'an. However, most of those verses are commands to the Prophet ﷺ himself, whereas this one is a command to him to convey to the believers that (instruction). This indicates that the verse was revealed at a time when the Muslims had grown in number and felt their strength. So they were commanded to pardon and to entrust the matter of their victory to Allah, the Exalted.

Even if it was revealed on a particular occasion that arose during the revelation of the surah, its relevance to the purposes of the surah is clear, for it is instruction in what suits the situation of the Muslims in Makkah among their opponents, and in bearing with their arrogance and tyranny until Allah judges between them.

Various reports have been narrated concerning its occasion of revelation, varying in weakness. Makki ibn Abi Talib related that a man among the polytheists insulted 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he intended to strike him. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This has not been authenticated. In al-Kashshaf it is said that a man of Ghifar insulted 'Umar, and he intended to strike him, and then it was revealed. And from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "We were in the presence of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when a reciter recited this verse, and 'Umar said: 'So that He may recompense 'Umar for what he did'" (meaning that it was the cause of the revelation of the verse).

Al-Wahidi and al-Qushayri related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq: they camped at a well called al-Muraysi'. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy sent his servant to draw water from the well, but he was slow. When he came, he said: "What is holding you back?" The servant of 'Umar said: "He sat at the mouth of the well and did not let anyone draw water until he had filled the water-skins of the Prophet ﷺ and the water-skins of Abu Bakr, and filled for his master." 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: "Our likeness and theirs is only as the saying goes: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.'" 'Umar ibn al-Khattab then intended to kill him, and it was revealed.

Ibn Mihran related from Ibn 'Abbas that when His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Who is it that would lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245] was revealed, Finhas the Jew said: "The Lord of Muhammad has become poor." When 'Umar heard of that, he wrapped his sword around himself and went out in search of him, and then it was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for him, and when he came, he said: "Put down your sword." These are two weak reports, and because of them it is narrated from 'Ata', Qatadah and Ibn 'Abbas that this verse is Madani.

The closest of these reports is what Makki ibn Abi Talib related. Even if they were authentic, there would be nothing in them that disrupts the coherence of the verses, whether its revelation coincided with that incident or Allah commanded its placement in this position.

The word ﴿يَغْفِرُوا﴾ (yaghfiru) is in the jussive mood, either by the assumed elided lam of command, meaning: "Say to them: let them forgive (li-yaghfiru)", or it is jussive as the answer to "say", with the spoken words elided and indicated by the answer. The estimate is: "Say to those who believe: forgive, they will forgive." This is a expression of confidence in the believers, that when the Messenger ﷺ tells them, they will comply. Both possibilities occur in such a construction wherever it appears in speech, and this was previously discussed at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Say to My servants who believe: let them establish the prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31] in Surah Ibrahim.

﴿Those who do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ is intended to refer to the polytheists of Makkah.

Al-raja' (expectation): the anticipation and seeking of a beloved matter. This is the most well-known usage of the term, and it is the apparent meaning in this verse.

Al-ayyam (the days): the plural of yawm (day). This plural, or its singular, when attached to the name of a person, a people or a tribe, means the day on which victory and dominance over an opponent or fighter occurred for the one it is attached to. From this, the famous battle days among the Arab tribes were called "the Days of the Arabs," meaning those in which fighting occurred between tribes, some of whom triumphed over others. Just as one says "the Days of 'Abs," "the Days of Dahis and al-Ghabra'," "the Days of al-Basus." 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"And days for us, bright and long, when we disobeyed the king in them, refusing to submit."

When they say "the Days of Banu so-and-so," they mean the days in which the one to whom the days are attached was victorious. And they say "the Days of Banu so-and-so over Banu so-and-so," meaning that the one governed by the preposition of elevation ("over") is defeated, because the word "days" or "day" implies the meaning of victory and triumph. By this implication the genitive was connected to the word "days" or "day," even though it is a fixed noun. So the meaning of "the Days of Allah" in this sense is of the same kind as their saying "the Days of Banu so-and-so." Thus the meaning of expecting (raja') is derived in its apparent usage.

The understanding of "the Days of Allah," according to the pattern of its like, is that the meaning of the verse is: "to those whose souls do not anticipate the Days of Allah's victory, that is, Allah's victory for them." Either because they do not rely upon Allah and do not seek His aid, but turn instead to the idols; or because it does not occur to them except that they are victorious by their own power and strength, so the thought of seeking Allah's victory or hoping for it does not come to their minds. They were known for this trait among the Muslims, and therefore it was attributed to them here and they were identified by it.

The identification of them by this attribute was chosen so that it would contain an allusion that Allah gives victory to those who expect the Days of His victory, and these are the believers. The purpose of this allusion, through the relative clause, is to indicate the reason why the believers are commanded to forgive the polytheists and to pardon the harm of the polytheists, and not to exert themselves to avenge themselves, because Allah has guaranteed them victory.

The expression "the Days of Allah" is sometimes used in the Qur'an for the days in which His bounty and blessing came upon a people; this is one of the two explanations of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 5].

The meaning of ﴿do not expect the Days of Allah﴾ according to this interpretation is that they are preoccupied, away from expecting Allah's blessings, by what they are engaged in, attributing the good to their idols and devoting themselves to worshipping idols instead of worshipping Allah. In this interpretation there is the same allusion and encouragement as in the first interpretation, because the believers are those who expect Allah's blessing. This interpretation is applied to His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us said﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], and His saying ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect for Allah any dignity?﴾ [Nuh: 13]. So the intended meaning of "the Days of Allah" is the days of His recompense in the Hereafter, because they are the days of the manifestation of His judgement and might; these are close to the days in the first meaning. From this is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿That is the true Day﴾ [al-Naba': 39], meaning: that is the day of victory which rightly deserves to be called a day. So the meaning of this verse is: they do not fear that Allah has power to punish them, because they do not believe in the Resurrection.

The meaning of the verse is that the believers were commanded to pardon the harm of the polytheists, and this is repeated in the Qur'an. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿You will surely hear much harm from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah. But if you are patient and fear Allah, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186]. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Usamah ibn Zayd concerning this verse: ("The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions used to pardon the polytheists and the People of the Book as Allah had commanded them, and they would bear patiently the harm.")

His saying ﴿so that He may recompense a people for what they used to earn﴾ is a reason for the command implied by His saying "let them forgive" (yaghfiru), meaning: let them forgive and overlook the harm of the polytheists, and not avenge themselves, so that Allah may recompense them for their faith and for what they were harmed for in His way. For taking vengeance for oneself is a fulfilment of one's right; but what could they attain of healing their souls by pursuing retaliation against the polytheists, given their small number and the great number of those others? When they rely upon the victory of their Lord, His victory for them is more complete and more effective in breaking the might of the polytheists, as Noah said: ﴿I am overpowered, so help [me]﴾ [al-Qamar: 10]. This is part of the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming, so forgive with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85]. The apparent construction would have been to say "so that He may recompense them for what they used to earn." Instead, the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun, so that the word "a people" (qawman) would indicate that they are not neglected in the sight of Allah, for the word "qawm" indicates a group that has its own standing and honour: ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾ [Muhammad: 11].

The indefiniteness of "qawman" is for magnification, as if it were said: "so that He may recompense whatever people," meaning particular people. This is praise of them and commendation of them. Similar to this is what al-Tibi related from Ibn Jinni, from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, concerning the words of the poet:

"Will the sons of Marwan take our blood unjustly, and by Allah, if they do not rule with just judgement?"

Abu 'Ali said: He, the Exalted, is the most definite of the definite, and the poet called Him "a just judgement," and he expressed the word in the form of indefiniteness. Do you not see how the speech moved from the form of indefiniteness to the meaning of definiteness? End of quote. The more apparent view is that "qawman" is intended to be vague, and its tanwin is merely for indefiniteness.

The meaning: so that Allah may recompense every people for what they earned of good or evil, in a manner suited to their earning. Thus it is a threat to the polytheists who transgress against the believers, and a promise to the believers who were commanded to overlook and pardon the harm of the polytheists. This is the reason the recompense is not connected to a pronoun of those who are certain, since generality is intended; there is no explicit noun in place of a pronoun. This is supported by His saying ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self; and whoever does evil, it is against it.﴾ This is like a detailing of the general statement in His saying ﴿so that He may recompense a people for what they used to earn﴾. For this reason the sentence is separated and not joined to what precedes it, and a parallel of this was discussed in Surah Fussilat.

The majority read ﴿li-yajziya qawman﴾ with a ya' at its beginning, and the hidden pronoun refers to the divine name in His saying "the Days of Allah." Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the nun of majesty at its beginning, as an iltifat (shift of person). Abu Ja'far read it with a ya' at its beginning, vowelled with a damma, and with a fatha on the zay, in the passive voice, and put "qawman" in the accusative. Its explanation is that the deputy of the subject is a verbal noun derived from the verb yajzi. The estimate: "so that the recompense may be recompensed." And "qawman" is the second object of the verb yajzi, following the pattern of kasa and a'ta. This is not the substitution of the verbal noun as an absolute object, which the grammarians of Basra forbade; rather, the verbal noun is made the first object in the pattern of a'ta, and in meaning it is the second object of the verb jazā. The substitution of the second object in the pattern of kasa and a'ta is agreed upon as permissible, although the more common practice is the substitution of the first object, as in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Then He will recompense him with the fullest recompense﴾ [al-Najm: 41].

"Then to your Lord you will be returned." That is, after your deeds in this world, you will come to the judgment of Allah the Exalted, and He will recompense you for your good and bad deeds in a manner that suits your deeds.

He described arriving at the judgment of Allah as a "return" (ruju') to Allah, in the manner of a parable: the case of one who was far from his master or his commander, who acted as he pleased, then returned to his master or commander, and so he meets the recompense for what he did. Similar examples of this have already passed.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah.

The meaning of Allah giving them these three things is: bringing them into existence within the community, and bringing into existence those who carry them out, because the benefit of this returns to the whole community. As for ﴿provided them with good things﴾, it refers to Allah making easy for them the possession of the land of al-Sham, which "flows with milk and honey" as in the Torah in the promise to Ibrahim, and to which the fruits of the neighboring lands are brought, and whose coastal harbors receive the merchandise of the nations facing them across the sea, so that its ports overflow with various kinds of food, clothing, fruits, produce, and adornments. This is due to the favorable location of the land between the East by land and the West by sea. "Al-tayyibat" (good things) are those that are pleasant to people, pleasing in taste, appearance, benefit, and adornment.

As for ﴿preferred them over the worlds﴾, it means that Allah combined for them uprightness of religion and morals, self-rule, the spread of the foundations of justice among them, and a good life, security, and prosperity. By "the worlds" is meant the nations of their time. All of this is a report about the past state of the Children of Israel at the height of their affairs, not about what their affair came to after they differed, their kingdom perished, and their law was abrogated.

"Bayyinat" is an adjective treated as if it were a noun: al-bayyinah is the manifest proof, i.e., We gave them proofs, that is, We taught them, through their books and through their scholars, the proofs of truth and guidance, which by their nature leave no paths open for doubt and error in their souls except that they close them.

"Al-amr" is the affair, as in His saying ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud: 97]. The definite article in "al-amr" is for magnification, i.e., of great affairs: the affair of the community and that by which its order is sustained, since Musa and the prophets after him left nothing important of their interests unexplained, unclarified, and without warning against confusion concerning it.

The consequent has been omitted, indicated by what follows it, in the manner of brevity, since the intended aim is to express wonder at their condition: how they differed when there was no reason for difference, since their disagreement occurred after the knowledge mentioned just before had come to them: the Book, the judgment, prophethood, and the clear proofs concerning the affair. This statement is a metonymic allusion (kinayah) to the absence of any wonder at the disagreement of the polytheists with the believers, since the polytheists are not upon knowledge or guidance, such that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would know that he was being wronged in his mission.

This injustice is the injustice of envy, for envy is among the greatest of injustices. The clause ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ﴾ is a resumed clause of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because their strange report arouses in the hearer's mind a question about Allah's recompense for them for their deeds. This is an answer that contains a general indication, to magnify what will be decided between them regarding good and evil, since disagreement implies one who is right and one who is wrong.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement and provided them with good things. They did not differ until knowledge came to them. Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ﴾ [Yunus: 93], in Surah Yunus.
