Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verses 18–19:

﴿Then We placed you upon a path (sharī'ah) of the command. So follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they will not avail you anything against God. Indeed, the wrongdoers are allies of one another, and God is the Ally of the God-conscious.﴾

**(ثُمَّ)** is used for graded sequence (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), as is its usual function in conjoining sentences. Were the graded sequence not intended, the sentence would have been conjoined with **الواو** (wa, "and"). This sequence indicates that the content of the sentence conjoined by **ثُمَّ** is more important than the content of the sentence it follows, in the way that the purpose is more important than the premise, and the conclusion more important than the proof.

In this graded sequence there is an honouring of this placing (jaʿl) and an indication that it is superior to the giving to the Children of Israel of the Book, the judgment, the prophethood and the clear proofs from the command. So the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, his Book, his judgment and his clear proofs are superior and more guiding than what the Children of Israel were given of the like.

**(عَلى)** is used for figurative elevation, meaning firm establishment and steadfastness, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah: 5).

The indefiniteness of **شَرِيعَةٍ** (sharīʿah) is for magnification, as indicated by the graded-sequence particle.

**The sharīʿah** (the path; religion and the followed creed) is derived from **الشَّرْعُ**, which is the making of a road for travel. The way is called **شَرْعًا** by naming it with the verbal noun. The water source that people come to is called **شَرِيعَةٌ** for this reason. Al-Raghib said: the name *sharīʿah* has been borrowed for the divine way, by analogy with the water source. I say: the point of resemblance is the benefits in water, namely quenching thirst and purification.

**The command** (al-amr) is the matter, and it is the matter of the religion, which is one of God's affairs. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ (al-Shura: 52). So **مِن** here is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), and it is not like the **مِن** in His earlier saying: ﴿And We gave them clear proofs of the command﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 17), because the annexation of **شَرِيعَةٍ** to **الأمْرِ** prevents that.

This sentence has reached a great level of conciseness, for it conveys that the sharīʿah of Islam is superior to the sharīʿah of Moses, that it is a great sharīʿah, and that the Messenger ﷺ is firmly established in it, and nothing shakes him from persistence in explaining it and calling to it.

For this reason, the command to follow it is made a consequence of this, in His saying: **"فاتَّبِعْها"** (so follow it), meaning: persist in following it. The imperative here seeks continuance, like ﴿O you who believe, believe in God and His Messenger﴾ (al-Nisa': 136).

Between His saying **"فاتَّبِعْها"** and His saying ﴿and do not follow the desires of those who do not know﴾ there is the embellishment of antithesis (muḥassin al-muṭābaqah), between the command to follow and the prohibition of following something else.

**"الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ"** (those who do not know) are the polytheists, and their desires are the religion of polytheism. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 23).

**الأهْواءُ** (the desires) is the plural of **هَوًى**, which is love and inclination. The meaning is that their religion consists of deeds they loved, which God did not command and which the proofs did not require.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended purpose is to make the polytheists hear it, lest they hope for accommodation from the Messenger ﷺ when they see him overlooking their lapses and their harm, and when they hear in the Qur'an the command to pardon them, as in the preceding verse: ﴿Say to those who believe: forgive those who do not expect the Days of God﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 14).

In it there is also an indirect address to the Muslims, that they should beware of the desires of those who do not know. From Ibn ʿAbbās: it was revealed when Quraysh invited him to the religion of his fathers. Al-Baghawi said: they used to say to him: return to the religion of your fathers, for they are better than you.

The clause **﴿إنَّهم لَنْ يُغْنُوا عَنْكَ مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا﴾** (Indeed, they will not avail you anything against God) is a reason (taʿlīl) for the prohibition against following the desires of those who do not know, and it implicitly contains the reason for the command to follow God's sharīʿah. For their not availing him anything against God entails that in opposing what God commanded, namely following His sharīʿah, there is what brings on God's anger and punishment, so following their desires does not avail him against His punishment.

**الإغْناءُ** (availing) is making another self-sufficient, that is, not in need. So the sinner threatened by one who is powerful is not self-sufficient with respect to the one who punishes him. Even if someone equal to his threatener, or stronger than him, protected him, he would still not be made independent of him. The verb **الإغْناءُ** is construed with the meaning of repelling, so it takes **عَنْ**. **"شَيْئًا"** is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), and **"مِنَ اللَّهِ"** is an adjectival qualifier of **"شَيْئًا"**. The **مِن** here is in the sense of substitution (badal): they will not avail you, as a substitute for God's punishment, anything of availing. That is, a little of substitute availing against God's punishment. So the statement is elliptical (ḥadhf muḍāf), and this was discussed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them anything against God﴾ (Al ʿImran: 10).

Another reason is conjoined to this reason, namely **﴿وإنَّ الظّالِمِينَ بَعْضُهم أوْلِياءُ بَعْضٍ﴾** (and indeed the wrongdoers are allies of one another). That is: they are wrongdoers, and you are not among the wrongdoers in any respect, so it is not permissible for you to follow them in anything. Only those whose allies they are follow them. He appended to this His saying: **﴿واللَّهُ ولِيُّ المُتَّقِينَ﴾** (and God is the Ally of the God-conscious), which indicates that the Prophet ﷺ is one whom God takes as ally, because the Prophet ﷺ is the foremost of the God-conscious.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verses 18–19:

﴿Then We placed you upon a path (sharī'ah) of the command. So follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they will not avail you anything against God. Indeed, the wrongdoers are allies of one another, and God is the Ally of the God-conscious.﴾

**(ثُمَّ)** is used for graded sequence (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), as is its usual function in conjoining sentences. Were the graded sequence not intended, the sentence would have been conjoined with **الواو** (wa, "and"). This sequence indicates that the content of the sentence conjoined by **ثُمَّ** is more important than the content of the sentence it follows, in the way that the purpose is more important than the premise, and the conclusion more important than the proof.

In this graded sequence there is an honouring of this placing (jaʿl) and an indication that it is superior to the giving to the Children of Israel of the Book, the judgment, the prophethood and the clear proofs from the command. So the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, his Book, his judgment and his clear proofs are superior and more guiding than what the Children of Israel were given of the like.

**(عَلى)** is used for figurative elevation, meaning firm establishment and steadfastness, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah: 5).

The indefiniteness of **شَرِيعَةٍ** (sharīʿah) is for magnification, as indicated by the graded-sequence particle.

**The sharīʿah** (the path; religion and the followed creed) is derived from **الشَّرْعُ**, which is the making of a road for travel. The way is called **شَرْعًا** by naming it with the verbal noun. The water source that people come to is called **شَرِيعَةٌ** for this reason. Al-Raghib said: the name *sharīʿah* has been borrowed for the divine way, by analogy with the water source. I say: the point of resemblance is the benefits in water, namely quenching thirst and purification.

**The command** (al-amr) is the matter, and it is the matter of the religion, which is one of God's affairs. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ (al-Shura: 52). So **مِن** here is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), and it is not like the **مِن** in His earlier saying: ﴿And We gave them clear proofs of the command﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 17), because the annexation of **شَرِيعَةٍ** to **الأمْرِ** prevents that.

This sentence has reached a great level of conciseness, for it conveys that the sharīʿah of Islam is superior to the sharīʿah of Moses, that it is a great sharīʿah, and that the Messenger ﷺ is firmly established in it, and nothing shakes him from persistence in explaining it and calling to it.

For this reason, the command to follow it is made a consequence of this, in His saying: **"فاتَّبِعْها"** (so follow it), meaning: persist in following it. The imperative here seeks continuance, like ﴿O you who believe, believe in God and His Messenger﴾ (al-Nisa': 136).

Between His saying **"فاتَّبِعْها"** and His saying ﴿and do not follow the desires of those who do not know﴾ there is the embellishment of antithesis (muḥassin al-muṭābaqah), between the command to follow and the prohibition of following something else.

**"الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ"** (those who do not know) are the polytheists, and their desires are the religion of polytheism. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 23).

**الأهْواءُ** (the desires) is the plural of **هَوًى**, which is love and inclination. The meaning is that their religion consists of deeds they loved, which God did not command and which the proofs did not require.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended purpose is to make the polytheists hear it, lest they hope for accommodation from the Messenger ﷺ when they see him overlooking their lapses and their harm, and when they hear in the Qur'an the command to pardon them, as in the preceding verse: ﴿Say to those who believe: forgive those who do not expect the Days of God﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 14).

In it there is also an indirect address to the Muslims, that they should beware of the desires of those who do not know. From Ibn ʿAbbās: it was revealed when Quraysh invited him to the religion of his fathers. Al-Baghawi said: they used to say to him: return to the religion of your fathers, for they are better than you.

The clause **﴿إنَّهم لَنْ يُغْنُوا عَنْكَ مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا﴾** (Indeed, they will not avail you anything against God) is a reason (taʿlīl) for the prohibition against following the desires of those who do not know, and it implicitly contains the reason for the command to follow God's sharīʿah. For their not availing him anything against God entails that in opposing what God commanded, namely following His sharīʿah, there is what brings on God's anger and punishment, so following their desires does not avail him against His punishment.

**الإغْناءُ** (availing) is making another self-sufficient, that is, not in need. So the sinner threatened by one who is powerful is not self-sufficient with respect to the one who punishes him. Even if someone equal to his threatener, or stronger than him, protected him, he would still not be made independent of him. The verb **الإغْناءُ** is construed with the meaning of repelling, so it takes **عَنْ**. **"شَيْئًا"** is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), and **"مِنَ اللَّهِ"** is an adjectival qualifier of **"شَيْئًا"**. The **مِن** here is in the sense of substitution (badal): they will not avail you, as a substitute for God's punishment, anything of availing. That is, a little of substitute availing against God's punishment. So the statement is elliptical (ḥadhf muḍāf), and this was discussed at His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them anything against God﴾ (Al ʿImran: 10).

Another reason is conjoined to this reason, namely **﴿وإنَّ الظّالِمِينَ بَعْضُهم أوْلِياءُ بَعْضٍ﴾** (and indeed the wrongdoers are allies of one another). That is: they are wrongdoers, and you are not among the wrongdoers in any respect, so it is not permissible for you to follow them in anything. Only those whose allies they are follow them. He appended to this His saying: **﴿واللَّهُ ولِيُّ المُتَّقِينَ﴾** (and God is the Ally of the God-conscious), which indicates that the Prophet ﷺ is one whom God takes as ally, because the Prophet ﷺ is the foremost of the God-conscious.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 20:

﴿This is clear evidence for mankind, and a guidance and a mercy for a people who have certainty.﴾

If the demonstrative refers to the preceding discourse, and what it contains of the parable of Musa and his people, and of the preference of the law of Muhammad over the law of Musa, peace be upon them both, and the command to hold fast to following it, and the warning against following the desires of those who do not know, then this sentence serves as a conclusion (tadhyil) to what came before it and as a preparation for its aims, drawing attention to what is within it of safeguards against doubt and falsehood. It is like His saying, exalted is He, after a number of verses at the end of Surat al-Ahqaf, ﴿a message (balagh)﴾, and His saying in Surat al-Anbiya':

صفحة ٣٥٠
﴿And We had already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105] ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾ [al-Anbiya': 106].

If the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an, as it is present in minds, then the sentence is a new resumptive statement by which the esteem of the Qur'an and of those who follow it is reiterated, with an allusion to deriding those who turned away from it. It would then confirm His earlier saying, ﴿This is guidance, and those who disbelieve in the signs of their Lord will have a painful punishment of wretched torment﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 11]. The earlier sentence would then be explicit in threatening those who disbelieve in His signs, while this one implies that they have not been granted these insights. Both possibilities are elegant, and each is rightly intended.

"Basa'ir" is the plural of basira, which is the perception by the intellect of matters as they truly are. It is likened to the sight of the eye, and the two are distinguished by the form fa'ila, for intensification. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to God with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾ [Yusuf: 108] in Surat Yusuf. And He said: ﴿He said: You know well that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ [al-Isra': 102] in Surat al-Isra'. And His saying: ﴿And We had already given Musa the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations, as insights for mankind﴾ [al-Qasas: 43] in Surat al-Qasas.

Describing the preceding verses or the Qur'an as "insights" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because they are the cause of insights. As for the plural of "basa'ir": if the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an in terms of those who gain insight through it, as His saying "for mankind" requires, then since each person has his own particular insight, it is a matter that is particular by way of consequence, since the possessor of each insight is a particular, individual person. Thus it was fitting to express it in the plural. The basira is a faculty among the inner senses. This differs from the singular form of "guidance and mercy," because guidance and mercy are universal meanings that can apply to a large number, as He, exalted is He, said: "guidance for mankind," and He said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

It was guidance because it is a path of benefit for whoever follows its direction, so following it is like being guided to the road that leads to the intended goal. It was mercy because in following its guidance lies the success of people, individually and collectively, in this world, since it is the order of their society and the basis of their security, and in the Hereafter, since it is the means of attaining the ranks of everlasting bliss. It was insights because it clarifies for people good and evil, encourages them to good, warns them against evil, promises them for doing good, and threatens them for doing evil, so its function is the function of insight.

صفحة ٣٥١
He made the insights for mankind because it is a clarification for people in general, and He made guidance and mercy for a people who have certainty because only one who is certain of its truth is guided by its clarification, and only one who follows it, believing in its truth, receives mercy from it.

The mention of the word "qawm" (a people) serves to indicate that certainty is firmly established in their souls, as though it were one of the constituents of their peoplehood that distinguishes them from other peoples.

Al-iqan (certainty) is knowledge about which its possessor has no doubt. Its object is omitted because it is known from what the signs of God have brought.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 21:

﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is what they judge.﴾

This is a transition from describing their denial of the signs and their mockery of them, then from the command to the believers to forgive them and to leave the requital of their deeds to God, then from the instruction to hold firmly to the Islamic law, to describing another kind of their misguidance and their mockery of the promise and the threat, and their claim that life after death and recompense for deeds are impossible, and their imagining to people that in the Hereafter they will be in the state they were in during this world: their great ones in the world will be great in the Hereafter, and their weak ones in the world will be weak in the Hereafter. This transition is a return to explaining His saying ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self; and whoever does evil, it is against it; then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 15].

So the particle (am) is for a transitional change of subject (idrab intiqali), and the interrogative that must be understood after (am) is a denying interrogative. The implied meaning is: "Do not those who commit evil deeds think that they are like those who believe, neither in life nor in death?"

As for ﴿those who commit evil deeds﴾, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the polytheists, as the shift from the previous theme to this theme indicates. He expressed them with this designation because of what the relative clause contains as a justification for denying similarity and equality between them and those who believe and do righteous deeds in the sight of God in the world of eternity. Also, the acquisition of evil deeds is a mark of the people of polytheism, since they have no religion restraining them from evil deeds, nor do they believe in resurrection and recompense, so that their belief in it would encourage them toward recompense. For this reason the Qur'an frequently uses the expression of being characterized by evil deeds as a metonymy for the polytheists, as in His saying ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1] up to His saying ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a great day?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4], and as in His saying ﴿What has caused you to enter Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddathir: 42] ﴿They will say: We were not of those who prayed﴾ [al-Muddathir: 43] ﴿Nor did we feed the poor﴾ [al-Muddathir: 44] ﴿And we used to plunge with the plungers﴾ [al-Muddathir: 45] ﴿And we used to deny the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Muddathir: 46], and His saying ﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾ [al-Ma'un: 1] ﴿For that is the one who drives away the orphan﴾ [al-Ma'un: 2] ﴿And does not encourage the feeding of the poor﴾ [al-Ma'un: 3]. Its counterpart is ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 4], for that is the condition of the disbelievers, whereas the sinning believer does not reach the state of thinking that he escapes God's power.

It is said: it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists. Al-Baghawi said: it was revealed concerning a number of the polytheists of Makkah who said to the believers: "If what you say is true, we will be given preference over you in the Hereafter just as we were given preference over you in this world."

And from al-Kalbi: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah said to 'Ali, Hamzah and some of the Muslims: "By God, you are not upon anything. If what you say is true (i.e., if resurrection is true), then our state will be better than yours in the Hereafter, just as we are in a better state than you in this world." The interpretation of the revelation of this verse according to this occasion of revelation is that the utterance of these people coincided with the time of the revelation of these verses of the surah, or that their saying was repeated, so it was appropriate for the verse to address it in its rightful manner.

The revelation of the verse according to this occasion is to refute their speech in its apparent state, even though they did not say it out of conviction but said it in mockery, so that their speech would not circulate among their rabble and the newly-converted in Islam, because the nature of one who undertakes guidance is that he leaves no opening through which falsehood might spread without blocking it, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: I will surely be given wealth and children?﴾ [Maryam: 77] ﴿Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78], and the Qur'an has many parallels to this.

Al-Qurtubi added, in relating the speech of al-Kalbi, that they said it when they confronted them on the day of Badr, but this is not sound, because the surah is Meccan and no one has reported an exception of this verse from it.

And al-Ijtirah means acquisition (al-iktisab), and the form of ifti'al in it is for emphasis; it is derived from al-jarh (wound). It was applied to the acquisition of beasts of prey and the like, which is why hunting dogs are called jawarih, and it was also applied to the acquisition of people, because most of their earning in the pre-Islamic period came from raiding the camels of a people, and that was with spears. Umm Zara' said: "Then she married after him a man of generosity, who rode a noble horse, took a spear, and brought me abundant camels in the evening," and for this reason the use of ijtiraḥ became predominant for acquiring sin and wrongdoing.

The apparent structure of the verse is that His saying ﴿equal in their living and their dying﴾ falls within the thing thought of as mentioned, so the meaning is: a denial that the polytheists be equal with the believers neither in life nor after death. Just as God made a difference between their two states in the life of this world, making one group disbelievers who do evil and another group believers who do good, so too He will make a difference between their two states at death: the polytheists will die in despair of God's mercy, since they do not have certainty about resurrection, and after death they will encounter the terror of what God has threatened them with; and the believers will die hoping for God's mercy and rejoicing in what they were promised, and after death they will encounter God's reward and His good pleasure.

The majority read "sawa'un" in the nominative, so the clause ﴿sawa'un mahyahum﴾ holds the position of a substitute for the kaf of comparison, which means "like," according to the view of the author of al-Kashshaf. He means that it is an exact substitute (badal mutabiq), since a clause may substitute for a singular noun according to the most correct view, and the exact substitute is, on careful analysis, the explicative apposition (‘atf al-bayan). Thus the clause ﴿sawa'un mahyahum wa mamatuhum﴾ explains what the polytheists supposed. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and Khalaf read it in the accusative, so the word sawa' alone is a substitute for the kaf of similarity, a singular substitute from a singular, or a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun of accusative in "naj'aluhum."

This is because the polytheists said to the Muslims: "We will be better than you after death just as we were better than you in life."

So the pronoun of "mahyahum" and the pronoun of "mamatihim" refer to each of those who committed evil deeds and those who believed, in distribution: the living of each is equal to its dying, meaning the state of the two groups does not change after death, but they will be after death as they were in life. However, the position of the particle of comparison in His saying "ka-alladhina amanu" is not clearly connected to the supposition of the polytheists on which the denial is directed, because they only supposed that they would be in a better state than the believers after death (on the assumption that resurrection occurs), not that they would be like the believers. They said this in the context of boasting over the believers and wishing to silence them with their sophistry. Therefore, we need to clarify the position of this kaf in the verse.

What I see is that its position is to indicate that God has decreed for the believers a good state after death, to the point that this decreed state became a standard for comparison and the basis of likeness; and also that the polytheists' supposition that they themselves would be in a good state in the Hereafter is false. So He expressed their false supposition by saying that they attributed to themselves in the Hereafter the state that belongs to the believers. That is, the polytheists supposed, according to their claim, that they would be after death in a state which, when the describer wishes to describe it, he describes by likening it to the state of the believers in the sight of God and in reality. The intended meaning is not that the polytheists made their state a likeness to the state of the believers, so that "ka-alladhina amanu" would be interpreted as a reporting of the speech by a phrase equivalent to it rather than by the words of its speaker. This is among the things in which latitude is allowed in reporting speech, as in His saying, exalted is He, quoting 'Isa: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: Worship God, my Lord and your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117], for what God commanded him was: "Worship God, your Lord and their Lord." This departs from the apparent requirement, and here God intended to honor the believers and to show care for their nearness to God. As if it were said: "Do they suppose that We will place them in a good state?" but this hoped-for state in their supposition is in reality the state of the believers, not their state. So the speech is concise, and the listener's understanding expands it.

The one addressed by this speech is the Prophet and the believers, completing the purpose introduced at the beginning in His saying ﴿Say to those who believe: forgive those who do not hope for the days of God﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14].

Moreover, you may take His saying "ka-alladhina amanu" as a parenthetical clause between the two objects of "naj'alu," which are the two pronouns of the absent, while the clause "sawa'un mahyahum" or the word "sawa'" in the reading of its accusative is not intended to be included in the supposition of the polytheists.

On this reading, "ka-alladhina amanu" may also be a mockery of the polytheists in their supposition, serving as an emphatic denial directed at them.

Among what is said against the apparent structure is that the content of "sawa'un mahyahum wa mamatuhum" is not part of the mentioned supposition of the polytheists, but is a new independent statement. The meaning is: when the denial of the supposition of equality between the disbelievers and the believers was made, it may occur to the hearer to ask how the actual state of the two groups is. So he is answered that the state of their living, which is the measure of the state of their dying, is different, that is, their state in the Hereafter is different just as it is different in this world. The believers live in turning toward their Lord and hoping for His grace, while the disbelievers live turning away from the worship of their Lord, despairing of resurrection and recompense. This is not the exact answer but is a sufficiency with the reason for the answer instead of mentioning it. The estimate is: the state of the two groups is different in the Hereafter just as it was different in life.

The clause ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ is a concluding summary of what precedes it, of the denial of their supposition and of the meanings connected to that denial.

Know that although the occasion of this verse concerns the difference between the states of the polytheists and the believers, the attaching of the judgment in it to the relative clause ﴿those who committed evil deeds﴾ makes it an indication of the difference between the states of evildoers and doers of good among the people of faith, even if no believer supposes that. It is reported from Tamim al-Dari that he spent a night reciting this verse, bowing, prostrating, and weeping until morning. Similar things are reported from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad: that he would often repeat this verse from the beginning of the night, then say: "Would that I knew to which of the two groups you belong," addressing himself. For this reason this verse was called "the weeping place of the worshippers" (mabka al-'abidin).

Al-Mahya and al-Mamat are two mimi verbal nouns or two nouns of time, meaning their living and their dying; and on both interpretations it implies an omitted genitive, that is, the state of their living and the states of their dying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 22:

﴿And Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾

This sentence is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), and the waw is a waw of parenthetical insertion (waw i'tiradiyya). It comes between the preceding discourse and what is built upon it, namely His saying ﴿Have you seen him who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. It serves as evidence for the negation that those who committed evil deeds, who live in ease during their lifetime, could be in bliss after their death, as those who believed and did righteous deeds during their lifetime, so that their recompense is bliss after their death. That is, after their second life, because the creation of the heavens and the earth in justice requires a difference between the one who does evil and the one who does good, and the vindication of the wronged against the wrongdoer.

The manner of the argument is that the creation of the heavens and the earth shows that He is in perfect mastery of craftsmanship and order, such that the indications of the will of justice are present in its transformations. What the Creator has deposited in His creatures of powers is suited to achieving that order in which their welfare lies. When they employ these powers in corruption and evil, it is part of completing the establishment of the order that they be punished for that evil. And it is observed that the evildoer often clings to his evil until death. Had there been no recompense after death, a disorder would have occurred in the order of the creation of creatures and the creation of the powers from which good and evil proceed. This meaning is repeated in many verses, and whenever some of it is mentioned, it is followed by mention of recompense. Already in Surat Al 'Imran His saying was mentioned: ﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; exalted are You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191], and His saying in Surat al-Dukhan: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39] ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 40].

The bi' in His saying bil-haqq is either causal (sababiyya) or accompaniment (mulabasa). That is, creating with a true cause, or accompanied by the truth, such that truth never departs from any of its states.

Al-haqq is a comprehensive term for that which by its nature is to be established and affirmed, and it is among the nature of wisdom and the Wise to establish it. For this reason it is indicated by His saying "And Allah created," since the Name of Majesty (Allah) comprises the attributes of perfection and the dispositions of wisdom.

The conjunction ﴿and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned﴾ is coordinated with "bil-haqq" because the coordinated element, the prepositional phrase with bi', carries the sense of causation (ta'lil). This is a detailed explanation after a general statement, since recompense for an action with what suits it is part of the truth. Also, the explanation of the creation by the cause of recompense is part of elaborating the meaning of truth and the effects of truth being the cause of the creation of the heavens and the earth, or accompanying the states of their creation. Thus the correspondence between the bi' in the first element and the lam in the coordinated element became evident.

The bi' in bima kasabat is for exchange (ta'wid). What a soul has earned is not recompensed by itself; rather it is repaid with its like and what suits it. So the speech contains an elision of a modifier, that is, "with the like of what it earned." This likeness is a likeness in kind, while the determination of the measure of that likeness is entrusted to Allah the Exalted, and it takes into account the magnitude of the world of recompense in good and evil, and the measure of the evildoer's rebellion and the good-doer's obedience. This differs from the prescribed punishments (hudud) and deterrents, for these are fixed by what suits the world of this life in its weakness.

For this reason He followed it with His saying: "and they will not be wronged." The pronoun in "hum" refers to every soul, for that recompense is among what justice requires, which has been made the cause of, or accompanying, the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is in them. So it is justice, and therefore it is not wrongdoing in any way. The one who is recompensed is not wronged. Also, through recompense the effect of the wrongdoer's injustice is removed from the wronged, for if recompense were abandoned, the wronged would remain wronged.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 23:

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god, and Allah has misguided him knowingly, and sealed over his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a covering? So who will guide him after Allah? Will you not then take heed?﴾

When those who thought that they would be in bliss and honour in the Hereafter, just as they had been in this world, said that without any proof or reasoning, but rather out of following what their souls desire of the continuance of the good state, the wonder at their condition was made to follow from their assumption. So the interrogative used for wonder was joined with the fa' (then), and it was made an interrogative about seeing their condition, to indicate that their condition had reached such a degree of manifestness that it could be seen.

The original structure is: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god﴾ and so on, with the interrogative hamza placed first. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is those with him among the Muslims; or the address is to an unspecified person, meaning that their state has become so manifest that it is not restricted to any particular addressee.

The relative "man" (مَن) applies to the group of mockers who thought that their living and their dying were equal, as indicated by the plural pronoun in the clause conjoined with the words ﴿And they say: there is nothing but our life of this world﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24], and so on.

The meaning is that their argument against the Muslims is centred on following desire and sophistry, so there is no standing up for their argument either in reality or in what they intended, on the supposition that resurrection occurs, that they would be safe from the terrors of resurrection, and that guidance is not hoped for them, because Allah created them unable to accept guidance, so no one other than Him can guide them.

"His god" (إلَهَهُ) may be understood as applied to that which his obedience is constantly bound to, so that it is as if it were a worshipped one; in that case this usage is by way of an eloquent metaphor, meaning that he took his desire as a god for himself, which does not oppose him in any command.

It is also possible that "his god" remains in its literal sense, and "his desire" (هَواهُ) means that which is desired, i.e., he worshipped a god because he loved to worship it. This refers to those who took idols as gods and do not desist from worshipping them because they loved them, meaning they became accustomed to them and their hearts became attached to worshipping them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93].

The meaning of "Allah has misguided him" is that He surrounded them with the causes of error, from obstinate intellects and weak souls which were accustomed to following what they desire and cannot bear patience and acceptance of what they dislike. So their hearing became as if sealed, in not benefiting from admonitions and proofs, and their hearts became as if sealed, in that the advice and indications of evidence do not penetrate them, and their sights became as if covered with veils, so they do not benefit from observing the divine creatures which indicate that Allah alone is God and that after this world there is a resurrection and recompense.

The meaning of "knowingly" (عَلى عِلْمٍ) is that the causes of error encompassed them while they were people of knowledge, i.e., of sound intellects; or, while knowledge of what would guide them had reached them, namely through the Qur'an and the call of the Prophet ﷺ to Islam.

Here the particle (عَلى) carries the meaning of accompaniment, in the sense of (مَعَ, with). The origin of this meaning is the metaphorical borrowing of the sense of elevation for figurative elevation, namely firm establishment between the attribute and the one attributed. This became widespread until it became one of the meanings of (عَلى), as in the saying of al-Harith ibn Hillizah:

"Certainly, upon hatred, there are fortresses and a firm, unbending might..."

The meaning is that he is astray while possessing the attribute of knowledge; knowledge here is part of the description of him who took his god as his desire, and he is able to attain knowledge, were he to strip himself of obstinacy and the inclination toward desire.

Al-Jumhur read "ghishawatan" (a covering) with a kasra on the ghayn and a fatha on the shin followed by an alif. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "ghishwatan" with a fatha on the ghayn and a sukun on the shin, and this is a case of naming by the verbal noun, which is a dialect.

The meanings of the seal and the covering were mentioned at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah.

From this relative clause is derived a denunciatory interrogative: whether anyone other than Allah is able to guide them. Its purpose is to console the Prophet ﷺ because of his intense grief over their conduct and their remaining in error.

"Min ba'di Allah" (after Allah) means: other than Allah. It was mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185], at the end of Surah al-A'raf.

From this is derived an interrogative about the addressees' failure to remember this truth, i.e., how did they forget it, to the point that they persisted in hoping for the guidance of those astray and grieved because the proof was of no avail with them? This is a denunciatory interrogative.

Some exegetes understood the relative "man" in His saying ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god﴾ as referring to a specific person. Muqatil said: it is Abu Jahl, on account of a conversation that took place between him and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, when they were circling (the Ka'bah) one night and they talked about the affair of the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, I know that he is truthful." Al-Mughirah said to him: "Enough! And what makes you think so?" He said: "We used to call him, in his youth, the Truthful and Trustworthy; but when his intellect matured and his judgement was complete, we call him the Liar and the Traitor?!" He said: "Then what prevents you from believing in him?" He said: "The daughters of Quraysh talk about me, that I have followed the orphan of Abu Talib for a morsel. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, if I follow him, never!" So this verse was revealed. If this is sound, then the correspondence of the account with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and Allah has misguided him knowingly﴾ is clear. Also from Muqatil: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, one of the mockers, who used to worship of the idols whatever his soul desired.

This verse is a foundation for warning against desire being the motive for believers in their deeds, so that they abandon following the evidences of truth. So if the truth is beloved to someone, that is from being characterised by love of the truth, following the proof, just as the believer loves prayer, congregation, the night prayers of Ramadan and the recitation of the Qur'an. And in the hadith: "Give us rest with it, O Bilal," meaning the iqamah for prayer. And from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "None of you believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought." And from Abu al-Darda': when a man rises in the morning, his desire, his deed and his knowledge are gathered together; if his deed follows his desire, then his day is a day of evil; and if his deed follows his knowledge, then his day is a good day.

As for following a beloved matter merely to satisfy the soul, without considering whether it is good or corrupt, that is the cause of error and of evil conduct.

'Amr ibn al-'As said:

"When a man does not abandon a food he loves, and does not restrain a misguided heart wherever it goes,
Then he is likely to meet, throughout time, a reproach which, when its like is mentioned, fills the mouth."

Among the transmitted sayings: "Three things are destroyers: a obeyed avarice, a followed desire, and a man's self-admiration." This is narrated as a hadith of weak chain.

The hearing is mentioned before the heart here, unlike the verse of Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts and over their hearing, and over their sights is a covering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], because the subject spoken of here, when it was said of them that they took their god to be their desire, it is established that they had bound their hearts to desire, and that binding was diverting the hearing from receiving the verses. So the hearing was placed first to convey that they are like one whose hearing is sealed; then "and his heart" was joined to it, completing it and reminding of that binding which diverts the hearing. Then "over his sight" was mentioned, in the sense of a covering-like veil, because what his heart was bound to blinded his sight from looking at the evidences of the created beings.

As for the verse of Surah al-Baqarah, the people spoken of there are those same people, but the discourse about them began with the equality of warning and not warning regarding them, in His saying ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. When its detail was intended, the sealing was placed first upon their hearts, because it is the origin, just as taking desire as a god was the origin in describing their state in the verse of Surah al-Jathiyah. So the state of the hearts is the origin of turning away from receiving and reflecting in both verses, but the arrangement of this verse follows the order required by the mention, while the arrangement of the verse of al-Baqarah follows what the natural disposition requires.

Al-Jumhur read "a fa-la tadhakkarun" (will you not then take heed) with a shaddah on the dhal. 'Asim read it with a single dhal (without shaddah).

Its original form, according to all, is "tatadhakkarun." As for al-Jumhur, their reading is by changing the second ta' into a dhal, because the two points of articulation are close, for the sake of lightness. As for 'Asim, his reading is by deleting one of the two ta's.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 45, verse 24:**

﴿They say, "There is nothing but our life of this world. We die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time." They have no knowledge of that; they only conjecture.﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) with the sentence ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think﴾ [al-Jathiya: 21]. That is, after they had argued with the Muslims that if there is a resurrection after death, then their final state will be better than the final state of the Muslims, they say this for the purpose of *tawarruk* (feigning a position in argument to gain the upper hand), while they do not truly believe in resurrection and recompense. Rather, they put it forward as a matter of dispute, and their real conviction is their saying ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world﴾.

Already in Surah al-An'am there occurred ﴿And they say, "There is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected"﴾ [al-An'am: 29]. The pronoun in *hiya* ("it") is the pronoun of the matter and the situation (*damir al-qissa wa al-sha'n*). That is, the matter of the discussion about resurrection is restricted to the claim that there is no life after death. In other words, the matter is the negation of resurrection, as the restriction of the matter to the life of this world indicates. That is, to the present life, which is near to us. So, they mean: do not prolong the debate with us over proving resurrection. It is also permissible for *hiya* to refer to "life" (*hayat*), by way of the implication of the exception (*istithna'*) on the presumed word "life." In that case, the restriction applies to the genus of life, confining it to the life of this world.

The clause ﴿We die and we live﴾ explains the clause ﴿there is nothing but our life of this world﴾. That is, there is no other world after this world; life is only the life of this world, and so when the one who was living dies, another comes to exist after him. The meaning of ﴿we die and we live﴾ is that some of us die and some live; that is, some remain alive until a term, or are born after those who have died. To indicate this continual renewal, the verb is expressed in the present tense (*al-fi'l al-mudari'*), meaning that life and death are renewed among us. So the meaning is: we die and we live in this present life, and there is no other life.

Then, if this clause is quoted in the very words of their speech, it may be that it was among the sayings that became a proverb (*mathal*) among them. If it is a report of the meaning of their speech, then it is an instance of the Qur'an's conciseness (*ijaz*), and they originally said: some of us die and some of us live, then (all) die; thus it became like a proverb.

It does not occur to the mind that the quotation of their words "we die and we live" requires the intention of "we live after we die," because their saying "there is nothing but our life of this world" turns the mind away from this. The conjunction with *wa* (and) does not require an order of sequence between the two conjoined elements in occurrence.

"We die" was placed first in the mention, before "and we live" in the explanation, although what is explained is their saying "there is nothing but our life of this world." It would have been apparent that the explanation should begin with the explained expression, so it would be said: "we live and we die." It is said that "we die" was placed first so that the *fasila* (the rhyming verse-end) could be achieved with the word "we live" alongside the word "the world" (*al-dunya*). In my view, the placing of the verb "we die" before "we live" is for the sake of emphasis on death in this context, because they are concerned with establishing that there is no life after death. Following this emphasis is the achievement of two *tibaq* (antitheses): between "our life of this world" and "we die," and then between "we die" and "we live." The *fasila* was achieved as a consequence. This is more befitting to the eloquence of the *i'jaz* (inimitability of the Qur'an). For this reason, it is followed by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they have no knowledge of that﴾. So the reference of "that" is to their saying ﴿and nothing destroys us except time﴾. That is, they have no knowledge that time is the one who causes death, since there is no evidence for it.

As for the addition of ﴿and nothing destroys us except time﴾, they intended to affirm the meaning that life and death are confined to this world, which they express by the term "time." So life comes by the creation of the form, and death by the action of time. How then can one who has been destroyed by time be expected to return alive? Time (*al-dahr*) is the continuous succession of its night and day.

The meaning is: our living ones proceed to death through the influence of time, that is, its occurrences, through a long duration that is followed by death through old age, or through causes that lead to destruction. Their statements on this are numerous. From ancient poetry is the saying of 'Amr ibn Qami'a:

*The daughters of time have shot at me from where I cannot see,*
*So what is the matter with one who is shot at and is not an archer?*

Perhaps they mean that if time were to have an effect, people would remain alive, as the Bishop of Najran said:

*The turning of the sun prevented survival,*
*And its rising from a place where it does not set.*

Since death is by the action of time, how can they be expected to return alive?

These were words that flowed on their tongues because of their scant reflection upon matters, even though they knew that God is the Creator of the worlds. As for what occurs in the world of transformations, they had no opinion about it, and how could they, given that their unlettered condition did not assist them in that? They would err in the details, to the point that they would produce what contradicts what they believe. For this reason, it is followed by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they have no knowledge of that﴾. So the reference of "that" is to their saying ﴿and nothing destroys us except time﴾. That is, they have no knowledge that time is the one who causes death, since there is no evidence for that. The rational proof shows that time, which is duration, does not cause death directly, which is evident, nor indirectly in causing death, since time is a conventional matter that does not act or influence. It is rather measures by which people gauge the intervals between events, and its reference is to the apportioning of the portion of day and night and the portions of the four seasons. The common people only imagined that time acts, and these are imaginations that spread until they settled in simple minds.

The meaning of "conjecture" (*zann*) in His saying ﴿they only conjecture﴾ is what is not knowledge; here it is imagination and supposition. The clause ﴿they only conjecture﴾ either explains the clause ﴿they have no knowledge of that﴾, or is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as if a questioner, upon hearing His saying ﴿they have no knowledge of that﴾, asked about their basis for saying that, and was answered that it is conjecture founded on imagination.

The imperfect verb is used in "they conjecture" because they continually renew this conjecture, and their young receive it from their elders across their generations, and they do not desist from it.

**[Page 363]**

This is a continuation of the commentary on verse 24 ("And they have no knowledge of that; they only conjecture"), so it is a coordinated clause: they adhered to the belief that there is no life after death, relying on illusions and imaginary analogies. When the verses of the Qur'an, clear in their indication of the possibility of resurrection and of its necessity, are recited to them, they do not counter them with anything that refutes them; rather they resort to bewilderment and say: "If the resurrection is true, then bring us our fathers, if you are truthful." So the intended "verses" are the verses of the Qur'an concerning resurrection, as indicated by what precedes and follows the statement.

صفحة ٣٦٤
In His saying ﴿Their argument was nothing but that they said, "Bring our fathers, if you are truthful"﴾ there is a recording against them of faltering away from clear proof, and resort to the weapon of the helpless: obstinacy, and departure from the sphere of inquiry.

The address in the imperative "bring" (ā'tū) is directed to the believers, with the Messenger ﷺ included. The phrase "except that they said" is an exception from "their argument," and it implies calling their statement an argument, though it is not an argument, since it is more akin to slander. Either the application of the name "argument" to it is by way of mockery of them, like the words of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hosted you, and we hastened your hospitality, before dawn, with a crushing sword, pounding."

Here he called killing "hospitality" (qirā). On this view, the exception in His saying ﴿except that they said, "Bring our fathers"﴾ is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil) used sarcastically.

Or the application of the name "argument" to their statement follows their own belief and assumption, without intending mockery of them; that is, they produced what they supposed to be an argument. In this case the application is a formal metaphor (isti'ārah ṣūriyyah), and the exception is likewise connected.

Or the application is a metaphor based on the relation of opposition (ʿalāqat al-ḍiddiyyah), so it is a sent metonymy (majāz mursal), by treating contrariety as if it were resemblance, with the intention of mockery. The meaning is then that they have no argument at all, since their only argument is this, and this is not an argument but obstinacy. Thus it results that they have no argument, by way of allusion and implicature (kināyah), like the words of Jiran al-'Awd:

"And a land in which there is no companion, except the wild oxen and the camels."

That is, there is no companionship in it whatsoever.

The phrase ﴿that they said, "Bring our fathers"﴾ may be parsed as occupying the place of nominative (raf') by the exception in the "emptied" construction (al-istithnā' al-mufarragh), according to all three considerations. It is then the subject of kāna, and "their argument" (ḥujjatahum) is its predicate, because "ḥujjatahum" is in the accusative in all of the widely known readings.

The fronting of the predicate of kāna before its subject is because its subject is restricted by "illā" (except), so its proper place is after the predicate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 26:

Page 365
﴿Say, "Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then gathers you for the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt, but most of the people do not know."﴾
This is an instruction (talqin) to refute their saying, ﴿And nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24], which includes the refutation of their saying, ﴿It is not but our worldly life; we die and we live﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24].

The purpose of it is His saying, "then causes you to die." Its being preceded by "gives you life" serves as a preparation for it (tawti'ah), meaning: just as He is the One who brought you into existence, He is the One who causes you to die, not time. So placing the name of Allah before the verbal predicate, "gives you life, then causes you to die," restricts giving life and causing death to Him, in refutation of their claim that time is what causes them to die.

His saying, "then gathers you for the Day of Resurrection," is a refutation of their saying, "It is not but our worldly life." It is not a refutation by way of argument, because the proofs for this had been repeated in what was revealed of the Qur'an, so the detailed presentation of them was dispensed with. Rather, it is a refutation by way of summary and counter-position (mu'aradah).

His saying, "about which there is no doubt," is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the Day of Resurrection, meaning: there is no doubt about its existence in light of what its occurrence requires, namely the bringing back of the dead. The meaning of the negation of doubt concerning it is that it is the true sense of doubt, which is constituted of indications leading to suspicion, and that this is negated from the matter of the occurrence of the Day of Resurrection, given the abundance of evidences indicating its possibility and that, with respect to the power of Allah, it is no more wondrous than the beginning of creation, and that Allah has informed us of its occurrence, so certainty of its occurrence is obligatory. Thus doubt about it deserves to be uprooted, and so it is as though it did not exist. This is like the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was asked about soothsayers: "They are nothing" (laysu bi-shay'), although they exist; he meant that they are not anything of real substance. This has already been discussed under His saying, "That is the Book about which there is no doubt" in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying, "but most of the people do not know," is conjoined to His saying, "about which there is no doubt," meaning: but the doubting of many people about it is because they do not know the proofs of its occurrence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verse 27–29:

[p. 366]
﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiraḍ tadhyīl) following His saying, ﴿Say: "Allah gives you life, then causes you to die"﴾ [al-Jathiya: 26]. That is: to Allah alone, and not to other than Him, belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. That is, He is the one who disposes of the affairs of whatever the heavens and the earth contain, of giving life and causing death, and of everything else, by what He brought into being of their origins and what He decreed of their causes and means. So neither time (al-dahr) nor anything other than Allah the Exalted has any disposal.

The placing of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) before the predicate (al-musnad ilayhi) serves to convey restriction (al-takhsis), to refute their belief that some of what is in the heavens and the earth is disposed of by other than Him, as in their saying about time (al-dahr):

* * *
﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day those who follow falsehood will lose﴾. ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling; every nation will be called to its record. Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿This is Our record, which speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We used to have copied what you were doing.﴾

When the mention of the Day of Resurrection came, it was followed by a warning to those who denied it of the evil of their end therein. Al-mubtiluna (those who follow falsehood) are those who engage in falsehood in their beliefs, their statements and their deeds, since falsehood is that which opposes the truth. The primary intended meaning here is polytheism (al-shirk) with Allah, for it is the greatest of falsehoods; then the degrees of falsehood descend in order, and every degree of it is a loss for its doer in proportion to his deed. Allah has warned people, and He is the All-Knowing of the measures of that loss.

﴿On the day the Hour is established﴾ is a temporal adverbial phrase governed by ﴿will lose﴾, and it is placed before it for emphasis on it and to draw attention to what follows concerning the description of its circumstances.

And ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ (on that day) is an emphatic restatement of ﴿the day the Hour is established﴾. Its tanwin is a substitute (iwaḍ) for the omitted genitive complement, the indication of which is what the word "day" is annexed to, i.e., "on the day when the Hour is established, those who follow falsehood will lose." So the emphasis is by confirming the content of the report and to magnify that day.

[p. 367]
The address in ﴿you see﴾ is to everyone who is fit to be addressed by the Qur'an, so no specific addressee is intended; it may also be an address to the Messenger (ﷺ). The present tense in ﴿you see﴾ is meant in the future sense, so the meaning is: "and you will see on that day."

Ummah (nation) is a great group of people united by a religion that a messenger brought to them.

Jathiyah (kneeling) is an active participle from the verbal noun al-juthuww (with two dammas), which is sitting on both knees in a crouched posture, i.e., without the buttocks touching the ground. So the jathi is one who sits crouched in a posture of submission.

The apparent sense of "its record" being singular and not defined with the article is that it is one record for each nation. This requires that the intended meaning is the book of the law, like the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel, the scrolls of Abraham and others, not the books of deeds. So the meaning of ﴿called to its record﴾ is: they are called to have their deeds presented against what they were commanded in their book, as in the hadith: "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you." It has also been said: what is meant by "its record" is the book recording the deeds of each individual, or it is meant as a generic noun, and its annexation to the pronoun of the nation is in the sense of distribution among the individuals, because each person of each nation has his own separate record of deeds, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra': 14], and He said: ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], i.e., every criminal is fearful of what is in his book. However, in this last verse the word "Book" came with the article, so generality was accepted. As for the verse of al-Jathiyah, its generality is partial (badali) by context. Thus what is intended is the specific nations to which messengers were sent and which had books and laws, according to God the Exalted's saying: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15].

The question of holding nations accountable whose messengers did not come to them, specifically regarding denial of God or associating partners with Him, is established in the principles of religion, and it was previously discussed at His saying ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15] in Surah al-Isra'.

The majority read ﴿every nation will be called to its record﴾ with kull (every) in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), and tud'a (will be called) as its predicate; the sentence is a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because the kneeling of the nation prompts the question of what comes after that kneeling.

[p. 368]
Ya'qub read it with kull in the accusative, as a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿And you see every nation﴾. The clause ﴿will be called﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿every nation﴾, so the phrase "every nation" is repeated rather than being satisfied with saying "will be called" — or it is for magnification. The calling to the record of the nations, which kneel and are then called, so each nation goes to its record for reckoning; that is, its members go to reckoning. Had it been said, "And you see every nation kneeling, called to its record," it would have given the impression that kneeling and being called to the record occur simultaneously, along with the magnification achieved by repeating the predicate a second time.

The clause ﴿Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿will be called to its record﴾, with an omitted verb of saying, i.e., it will be said to them: "Today you will be recompensed," meaning your recompense will be according to your deeds and their course in conformity with what agrees with the record of your religion of your actions, good and bad. This substitute came as a parenthesis between ﴿And you see every nation kneeling﴾ and the clause ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 30] and what follows.

The clause ﴿This is Our record, which speaks against you with truth﴾ is part of the implied statement, and it is a resumed explanatory sentence (istinaf bayani) anticipating the question of one of them who says: "What is the means by which their deeds are established?"

The demonstrative ﴿This﴾ refers either to the law-book of the community being called, or to the individual books of its members, interpreting "the book" as a generic noun, on the two aspects mentioned above.

The singular form of the verb ﴿speaks﴾ on this interpretation is in consideration of the wording ﴿Our record﴾; the meaning is: "these are Our books, which speak against you with truth."

The annexation of "record" to the pronoun of Allah the Exalted, after it had been annexed to each nation, is due to differing relations: the record is connected to the nation because it was made for counting their deeds, or because what they were charged with is recorded in it; and its annexation to Allah's pronoun is because He is the one who commanded it.

The attribution of speech to the record is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli); it is actually the angels of reckoning who speak according to what is in the record, or speech is borrowed to mean indication, as in the saying: "the situation spoke."

[p. 369]
The meaning: that in it there is testimony against them that their deeds contravene the precepts of the book, or that they are written in the scrolls of their deeds, on the two interpretations of what is meant by "the book."

Because "speaks" includes the sense of (yashhadu, "bears witness"), it is followed by the preposition (ʿalā, "against").

Since the context is one of threat, only "speaks against" with (ʿalā) is used without adding "for you" (wa-lakum), preferring the aspect of threat.

The expression ﴿will admit them into His mercy﴾ comprises whatever the soul can imagine of kinds of honor and bliss, since Allah's mercy is made like a place they enter.

The omitted element was not taken into account, because the advancing is to avoid the verbal awkwardness of the interrogative being after the particle, and this awkwardness still exists after what was omitted has been omitted.

The interrogative is rebuke and reproach. When they were lodged in Hell and it encompassed them, they were called: ﴿Today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this your Day, and your abode is the Fire, and you have no helpers.﴾ ﴿That is because you took the signs of God in mockery, and the worldly life deceived you. So today they will not be brought out from it, nor will they be granted the chance to make amends.﴾

This is for their despair of pardon from Him.

The verb ﴿qīla﴾ ("it was said") is in the passive voice, lowering them from the rank of being addressed directly by the name of God in the report of the speech that confronted them, as we pointed out earlier at His saying: ﴿And when it was said, "Indeed, the promise of God is true"﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32].

This is based on the view that the pronoun in ﴿nansākum﴾ ("We forget you") refers to God, and is not part of the speech of the angels. If it is part of the speech of the guardians of Hell, the verb ﴿wa-qīla﴾ is passive because the agent is known.

The word "forgetting" (nisyān) is used for lasting abandonment by way of metonymy (majāz mursal, a figure in which a word is used for something associated with its meaning), because forgetting implies leaving the forgotten thing in its place or leaving it in its state. It is also possible that "forgetting" is used metaphorically for neglect and indifference, meaning that the will is not directed toward lightening their condition. The second instance of "forgetting" is explained according to these two senses.

The particle "ka" in ﴿kamā nasītum liqā'a yawmikum﴾ ("as you forgot the meeting of your Day") denotes cause, as in His saying: ﴿And remember Him as He guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]. The meaning is: as a recompense for your forgetting this Day, that is, your turning away from belief in it.

"Liqā'" (meeting) means the finding of one thing with another in a place, and it is encounter. One says: Zayd met ʿAmr (laqiya Zaydun ʿAmran), and the sparrow found a grain (laqiya al-ʿuṣfūru ḥabbatan).

As for "the meeting of the Day": the Day is used for what occurs in it of events, by way of metonymy, because this is more concise than enumerating the terrors that take place from the Resurrection until the judgment of deeds is carried out.

The attribution of "Day" to the pronoun of the addressees in "yawmikum" (your Day) is because that Day is a time-frame for conditions connected to them, since attribution (iḍāfa) occurs for the slightest connection. Do you not see that it is attributed to the pronoun of the believers in His saying: ﴿And the angels will meet them: "This is your Day which you were promised"﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 103]?

Describing the Day with a demonstrative ("this Day") distinguishes it most completely, completing its definition by the attribution, lest it be confused for them with another day.

"And your abode is the Fire" is conjoined to "today We forget you" so that they may know that their abandonment in the Fire is an everlasting abandonment. The "abode" (ma'wā) is the dwelling of a person to which he returns after his deeds. The meaning is: you have taken refuge in the Fire, so you will remain in it. A similar expression to His saying ﴿and you have no helpers﴾ occurred shortly before. The aim is to refute their earlier claim that the idols benefit them in hardships.

"Dhālikum" (that) refers to "your abode", and the "bāʾ" (with) is causal, meaning: that abode is because of your taking the signs of God, which are the signs of the Qur'an, in mockery, that is, made the object of mockery. "Huzuan" (mockery) is a verbal noun used with the sense of the passive participle, like "khuluq" (creation/character).

The deception of the worldly life towards them is also a cause for making the Fire their abode.

"Taghrīr" (deception) is false enticement. The meaning of the worldly life deceiving them is that they measured the conditions of the Hereafter by the conditions of this world, so they thought that God does not give life to the dead. From this they proceeded to deny recompense in the Hereafter for what is done in this world. Also deceiving them was what they had of might and strength, so they took it to be the peak of perfection. Thus they did not give ear to the call of right guidance and the admonition of sincere counsel, and they turned away from the Messenger (ﷺ) and from the guiding Qur'an. Had it not been for this, they would have turned to reflect on what they were called to, and been guided, and so been saved from the consequences of disbelief. And because these deceptions are present in the worldly life, the deception is attributed to life by way of rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī, a figure in which an action is attributed to something other than its real agent), since that is more comprehensive of the causes of delusion.

On this basis: ﴿So today they will not be brought out from it﴾ is linked by "fa" (so), and this is part of the speech that was said to them, because the occurrence of the word "today" in its midst indicates that it is part of the saying that is addressed to them on that day. The readers agreed on reading "lā yakhrujūna" with the "yāʾ" of the third person. The apparent expectation was that it would be said "lā takhrujūna" in the second person, like what precedes it, but it turned from the mode of address to the third person by way of iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person). **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 45, verses 36–37:**

﴿So to Allah belongs all praise, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs grandeur in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Almighty, the Wise.﴾

The *fa'* (so) introduces the praise and commendation of Allah as a consequence of what the surah contains of Allah's kindnesses in what He created, guided, subjected and established of systems of justice, and His bounty upon the Muslims in this world and the Hereafter, and of His warning to those who turn away and of His argument against them. Since all of that comes from Allah, it indicates that He is described by attributes of greatness and majesty, and that He bestows favour upon people through the religion of Islam. Therefore He is deserving of the restriction of praise to Himself (*qasr al-hamd*). This statement may be intended in its apparent informative sense, and it may also be used with its allusive meaning (*kinā'ī*), which is the command to people to restrict praise to Him. It may also be an act of praising (*inshā'*) Allah the Exalted and extolling Him. Everything that preceded in the verses of this surah requires all three aspects. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-An'am: 45] in surah al-An'am.

The placing of *lillah* (to Allah) before the predicate serves to convey exclusivity (*ikhtisās*), meaning that praise is exclusively for Allah the Exalted. That is, true and complete praise belongs exclusively to Him, the Exalted, as was explained earlier in surah al-Fatihah.

The description "Lord of the heavens" being applied to His name, the Exalted, is an indication of the reason for restricting praise to Allah, both informatively and in act of praising, as an emphasis on what the *fa'* in His saying "so to Allah belongs all praise" required. "And Lord of the earth" is conjoined by repeating the word "Lord" in order to draw attention to the matter of lordship (*rubūbiyyah*), because the Lord of the heavens and the earth deserves to be praised by the people of the heavens and the earth. As for the people of the heavens, they have indeed praised Him, as Allah informed about them in His saying: ﴿And the angels glorify the praise of their Lord.﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. As for the people of the earth, whoever among them praises Him has fulfilled the right of lordship, and whoever praises other than Him and turns away from Him has marked himself with the mark of runaway slaves, and his destination is the Fire, the place of deserved punishment.

[Page 378]

Then it is followed by the description "Lord of the worlds," and they are the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, as an emphasis that they are entitled to praise Him, because He is the Creator of the worlds from which they benefit and the Creator of their own selves therein, likewise.

He follows that with the sentence ﴿And to Him belongs grandeur in the heavens and the earth﴾, to indicate that His summoning His creation to praise Him is only for their benefit and the purification of their souls, for He is independent of them, as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56] ﴿I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 57].

The placing of the prepositional phrase in "And to Him belongs grandeur" is like its placing in "So to Allah belongs all praise". *Al-kibriyā'* (grandeur) is true greatness, which is the perfection of attributes and the perfection of existence.

Then this is followed by the two attributes, the Almighty and the Wise, because might (*'izzah*) includes the meanings of power and free choice, and wisdom (*hikmah*) combines the meanings of complete and comprehensive knowledge.

With this conclusion, the discourse announced the end of the surah, and this is among the excellences of the endings of surahs.
